interest: For diplomatic and legal historians, this file provides a granular look at the mechanics of interwar U.S.–Japan relations, showing how routine administrative friction over taxation forced major domestic statutory reform (the Act of August 27, 1935) to codify reciprocal privileges for unaccredited foreign officials. The extensive rosters and departure clearances offer exceptional prosopographical and intelligence insight into the vast network of Japanese military inspectors, technical experts, language officers, and commercial representatives operating across the United States during the escalation toward World War II. Furthermore, the documents illuminate the sharpening boundaries between legitimate governmental functions, commercial enterprise, and foreign political influence—exemplified by the State Department's denial of tax exemption to tourist bureau officials, counter-boycott funding concerns, and field investigations of Japanese trade federations and radio propaganda on the eve of the Pacific War.
overview: This file (Decimal File 894.01B, September 17, 1934 – May 10, 1939) documents the diplomatic, administrative, and statutory efforts of the United States and Japan to resolve the tax liability of non-diplomatic government personnel stationed in each other's territories. Sparked in late 1934 when the U.S. Treasury Department required departing Japanese railway official Yorio Yamamoto to post a surety bond, the correspondence traces interdepartmental collaboration between the State Department, the Treasury, and Congress that led to the passage of H.R. 7998 (enacted August 27, 1935) and subsequent codifications under Section 116(h) of the Revenue Acts of 1934, 1936, and 1938. Over the next five years, the file details regular exchanges between the Japanese Embassy and the State Department certifying reciprocal exemptions, issuing departure sailing permits, processing tax refunds, and managing rosters of Japanese naval and army ordnance inspectors, railway technicians, agricultural researchers, monopoly agents, exposition representatives, and language officers, alongside reciprocal reporting arrangements for American personnel across Japan, Korea (Chosen), and Taiwan. In addition to tax administration, the later sections of the file chronicle growing U.S. surveillance and regulatory scrutiny over Japanese propaganda and quasi-official trade bodies, featuring investigative inquiries into the Japan Foreign Trade Federation, propaganda broadcasts under the Espionage Act of 1917, and an official 1938 register of foreign agents registered under the newly enacted Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).
